title: Gethsemani, December 1941
hookLine: he enters a silent Cistercian abbey in the Kentucky hills

lines: A GATE IN THE KENTUCKY HILLS.
cards: December 1941. The whole country is loud. Pearl Harbor has just been bombed, and every radio is talking about war.

A twenty-six-year-old English teacher gets off a train in Kentucky, in the dark, with a small suitcase. He's given away most of what he owns. He rides out through frozen hills to a gate in a stone wall and rings the bell.
On the other side, men pray through the night, work the fields, and barely speak. He'll belong to that place for the rest of his life. Today: into the silence.

teach.b: First, the place. The Abbey of Our Lady of Gethsemani, near Bardstown, Kentucky, founded in 1848 by monks from France and named for the garden where Jesus prayed the night before he died.
Merton had made a retreat there that spring, in Holy Week, and wrote that it was the center of America. He arrived to stay on December 10, 1941. Second, the name.
The monks are Cistercians of the Strict Observance, nicknamed Trappists after the abbey of La Trappe in France, where a seventeenth-century reform called monks back to a hard, simple life.
They follow the Rule of Saint Benedict, written in the sixth century: prayer, work, reading, and a lot of quiet.

teach.h: NO VOW OF SILENCE, BUT ROOM.
teach.b: Third, the silence. In Merton's day, Trappists spoke almost never. They used a simple sign language for work, ate no meat, slept in their habits, and rose in the middle of the night to sing.
The surprise: there's no vow of silence. Their vows are obedience, stability, staying in one community for life, and conversion of life. Silence isn't a rule for its own sake.
It's room. Lamentations puts it in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is good to wait with silence for the salvation of God." Fourth, the new life.
Merton got a new name, Brother Louis.

teach.h: IT IS GOOD TO WAIT WITH SILENCE.
teach.b: The loud, funny, restless young man had found a place where he could finally stop talking and listen. He wouldn't stay quiet on paper, as you'll see. But he stayed.

how: Trappist monks and nuns still live by the Rule of Saint Benedict, rising in the night for prayer, and many monasteries, including Gethsemani, welcome guests on silent retreats.

games.q: it's December 1941. the country is going to war, and you've felt drawn to a silent monastery. what do you do?
o: wait until the war is over
take the train to Kentucky and ring the bell
stay a teacher and visit on retreat
games.why: Merton arrived at Gethsemani on December 10, 1941, three days after Pearl Harbor, and stayed a monk of that house for the rest of his life.

practice: For two minutes, make no sound on purpose: phone face down, no humming, no narrating, just the room as it is, the fridge, a car outside, your breath.
When your mind starts talking, let it talk and don't answer; monks treat silence as attention, not emptiness. If you pray, let this be the whole prayer.

wordCard.voice: Trappist. A monk or nun of the Cistercians of the Strict Observance, named for the abbey of La Trappe. Prayer, work, and deep quiet. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew/Aramaic behind Gethsemane: most likely 'oil press', the garden named in the abbey's name.
